screens.title: Deploying and Interacting with Your First Program
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you'll learn the practical, repeatable workflow for taking an Anchor Rust program from source code to a running program you can call from a client. We'll cover compiling your Rust into BPF bytecode using the Anchor toolchain, running a local Solana validator so you can test without network fees, and deploying the compiled program with anchor deploy. Then we will walk through writing a minimal TypeScript client that uses the generated IDL to build and send transactions, and finally how to fetch on-chain account state to assert behavior. This matters because development speed and confidence come from a tight loop: change code, build, deploy locally, run tests, and inspect state. A concrete example you'll follow is the my-counter-app — we build it with anchor build, run solana-test-validator, deploy with anchor deploy, then use a TypeScript test to initialize and increment a counter account and assert its value. Common pitfalls include forgetting to build before deploying, not starting the local validator, or not including required signers when creating accounts. By the end you'll understand the commands, the artifacts produced like. so and IDL files, and the client calls you need to send instructions and read program state. Ready to start this practical workflow and see a program run locally?

Module 4 › Chapter 3.4 › Deploying & Interacting
What you'll do in this chapter

Compile Anchor programs to BPF, run a local validator, deploy with Anchor CLI, and build a TypeScript client that sends transactions and reads account state.

Compile
anchor build -> .so in target/deploy and IDL in target/idl
Local Validator
Run solana-test-validator for isolated testing and a faucet.
Deploy & Test
anchor deploy, then run anchor test and client calls using the IDL.
Artifacts to inspect
  • .so file in target/deploy/
  • IDL JSON in target/idl/
  • Program ID reported by anchor deploy
Why this matters

Local deploy lets you iterate quickly and test program logic end-to-end with client code before you touch public clusters. The IDL bridges your on-chain program and TypeScript tests, giving typed access to instructions and accounts.

Explore Key Topics
Follow the build → deploy → test loop: compile to BPF, start a local validator, deploy, then interact via a typed client using the IDL.
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass
anchor build
Compiles Rust to BPF and emits .so and IDL
solana-test-validator
Local cluster + faucet for quick tests

Always run anchor build after code changes and before anchor deploy. Forgetting to rebuild is a common cause of stale deployments.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Part 1
screens.narratorSegment: These objectives map to the hands-on workflow you'll practice. First, you will compile an Anchor program into BPF bytecode so it can run on Solana. That includes running anchor build and inspecting the produced. so and IDL files to confirm the program's interface. Second, you'll set up a local Solana validator using solana-test-validator. This creates an isolated, resettable blockchain environment with a faucet so you can test transactions without real funds. Third, you'll deploy an Anchor program to that local validator using anchor deploy and ensure the program ID is written or updated in Anchor. toml. Fourth, you'll write a basic TypeScript client that uses anchor. workspace and the generated IDL to construct and send instructions. Each objective emphasizes not just the command but why it matters: compilation produces the runnable artifact, the validator protects the public network and accelerates iteration, deploy publishes your code to the cluster you control, and the client connects on-chain logic with UI or tests. As you study, think about what could go wrong at each step and how logs, CLI output, and the IDL help you diagnose problems.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Part 2
screens.narratorSegment: This second objectives panel emphasizes the practical skills for testing and diagnosing issues. You'll run anchor test to execute TypeScript tests against your local validator, observe msg! logs emitted by the program, and confirm assertions using fetched account state. You'll also practice error testing: how to create a scenario that triggers a program-defined error, such as a counter overflow, so you can verify custom error handling in your program. Finally, you'll practice the iterative loop of editing Rust code, running anchor build, deploying to the local validator, and re-running tests to confirm fixes. Knowing how to reproduce an error locally and how to read the CLI output reduces debugging time. A common misconception is treating anchor deploy as a substitute for anchor build; remember that deploy sends whatever is already built, so always build after source changes. These objectives prepare you to run reliable local experiments and to write client code that intentionally validates program behavior.

Testing and Iteration Objectives

screens.title: Compilation: anchor build and BPF bytecode
screens.narratorSegment: Compilation transforms your human-written Rust code with Anchor macros into the binary format Solana nodes execute. When you run anchor build, Anchor orchestrates a Rust cargo build that targets BPF, producing a shared object file — the. so — and a generated IDL JSON that describes your program's public interface. The. so is the deployable executable that the cluster stores and runs. The IDL is a machine-readable contract: it lists instructions, each instruction's accounts and types, and any custom errors. A practical example is the my-counter-app: after a successful build you will find a my_counter_app. so file in target/deploy and an IDL at target/idl/my_counter_app. json. Inspecting the IDL helps client code know how to marshal arguments and which account addresses to include. A common misconception is that only the. so matters. In practice, the IDL is equally important for client development because it enables typed clients via anchor. workspace and prevents malformed transactions. As a quick check, build your program and verify both artifacts exist. If compilation fails, read Rust compiler messages and Anchor attribute hints; they usually tell you which module or attribute caused the error. The key takeaway is: build produces both runtime code and the contract description you need for client-side interaction.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.4 › Compilation
What anchor build does

anchor build runs cargo build for BPF, producing a shared object (.so) and a generated IDL JSON that describes instructions, accounts, and errors.

Command
anchor build
Artifacts to verify
  • .so file in target/deploy — the executable bytecode
  • IDL JSON in target/idl — the program interface used by clients
Key Takeaway

Both .so and IDL are required: .so runs on the cluster, IDL lets clients construct valid instructions.

Example: file locations
target/deploy/my_counter_app.so
target/idl/my_counter_app.json
Confirm these files after a successful build. If you do not see them, check compiler errors and Anchor attribute usage.
Common mistake
Assuming deploy will rebuild. You must run anchor build after code edits so the .so matches your source before running anchor deploy.
Why the IDL matters
The IDL describes account layouts and instruction signatures so TypeScript clients can create transactions with correct arguments and account metas.

screens.title: Running a local validator
screens.narratorSegment: A local validator gives you a private Solana cluster on your machine for development and testing. To start, open a terminal and run solana-test-validator. This spins up a node with a faucet so you can request test SOL and it runs in a temporary ledger that resets when you stop it. While it's running, configure your Solana CLI to use the local endpoint with solana config set --url localhost, and confirm using solana config get. The benefit is immediate feedback: transactions you send from a client or anchor test execute quickly and you can inspect msg! logs. A common practical concern is ledger persistence: by default the test validator is ephemeral; if you need a persistent ledger you can pass flags to save the ledger to disk. Another misconception is believing the validator replicates network conditions exactly — it does not emulate mainnet traffic, but it provides a safe, isolated environment for functionally testing program logic. Example use: start the validator, deploy your compiled. so with anchor deploy, then run anchor test or your TypeScript client to verify initialization and increments. Closing question: when you see an RPC connection error, what three CLI checks will you perform first to ensure the validator is reachable?

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.4 › Local Validator
Start the local validator

Run the validator in its own terminal and keep it running while you deploy and test.

Commands
solana-test-validator
solana config set --url localhost
solana config get
Checklist if you see connection errors
  • Is solana-test-validator running?
  • Does solana config get show localhost as the RPC URL?
  • Are there firewall or port issues preventing local RPC connections?
Practical notes
The local validator includes a faucet so your test wallet can receive SOL for transactions. It is ephemeral by default; you can configure ledger persistence for longer-lived experiments.
Common misconception
The local validator is not a perfect replica of public networks. It is intended for functional testing, not performance or stress testing against mainnet conditions.
Key Takeaway

Use solana-test-validator and configure your CLI to localhost for fast, isolated testing and to capture program logs during development.

screens.title: Deploying with Anchor CLI
screens.narratorSegment: Deployment publishes your compiled. so to a configured Solana cluster. Using Anchor's CLI, anchor deploy reads your Anchor. toml to determine program IDs and the keypairs used for deployment. When you run anchor deploy against a local validator, Anchor will upload the. so and sign the deployment transaction with the provided keypair. For a fresh deployment Anchor may generate and then update Anchor. toml with the program ID. A practical example is deploying the my-counter-app: ensure you have run anchor build, that solana-test-validator is running, and that the Solana CLI points to localhost. Then run anchor deploy from the project root. Watch the CLI output for the Program ID and any error messages. A frequent mistake is deploying an out-of-date. so because the developer skipped anchor build after changes. Another point: Anchor handles signing and keypairs for you, but be aware of which keypair is used for deployment and where it is stored. After a successful deploy, your program is live on your local validator and ready to receive instructions from a client or tests. Ask yourself: did the deploy output a program ID and did Anchor. toml reflect it?

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.4 › Deployment
Deploy with Anchor CLI

Run anchor deploy from your project root after a successful anchor build and with the validator running.

Example command
anchor deploy
What to watch
  • Program ID printed by the CLI
  • Anchor.toml updated for fresh deployments
  • Any keypair or signing errors in output
Practical checks
Confirm your .so was built recently and that the validator is reachable before deploying. Check Anchor.toml to ensure the program ID matches the deployed program if you rely on a fixed ID.
Common mistake
Deploying without rebuilding leads to a mismatch between source and deployed behavior. Always run anchor build after edits.
Key Takeaway

anchor deploy publishes the compiled .so to the configured cluster and writes or updates the program ID so clients can target it.

screens.title: Client basics: Anchor TypeScript setup
screens.narratorSegment: The Anchor client stack provides utilities that make calling your deployed program straightforward. In TypeScript, anchor. AnchorProvider. env() constructs a provider that ties together a connection, a wallet, and default options. When you call anchor. setProvider(provider), Anchor's client functions will use that environment for RPCs. Most importantly, anchor. workspace. MyCounterApp is a typed object generated from the IDL that exposes program methods and account accessors. This typed workspace saves you from manually constructing instruction data and account metas. For example, after setting the provider, you can get the program reference: const program = anchor. workspace. MyCounterApp as Program. From there, program. methods. initialize() builds the initialize instruction according to the IDL. A common misconception is that you can call methods without the IDL; while possible manually, the IDL ensures argument order and account names match the program. A concrete scenario: generate a counterAccount keypair, call initialize with signers([counterAccount]), then fetch the account with program. account. counter. fetch(counterAccount. publicKey) to read the count. When tests run with anchor test, Anchor sets environment variables so provider. env picks up the localhost cluster automatically. Reflect: how does the IDL reduce mistakes when building transactions?

keyIdea.text: anchor.AnchorProvider and anchor.workspace use the IDL to give you typed access to program methods and account fetch helpers.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.4 › Client Basics
Provider and workspace

Use anchor.AnchorProvider.env() and anchor.setProvider(provider) to configure the client for the local cluster, then use anchor.workspace to access your program via the IDL.

Key snippet
const provider = anchor.AnchorProvider.env();
anchor.setProvider(provider);
const program = anchor.workspace.MyCounterApp as Program;
Why this helps
The IDL-driven workspace prevents account ordering and argument-mismatch errors that commonly occur when constructing instructions by hand.
Example flow
Generate a Keypair for a counter account, call initialize with that public key and include it in signers. Later fetch the account via program.account.counter.fetch to inspect the count.
Common mistake
Omitting the new account in signers when using #[account(init)] will cause the transaction to fail because the account's keypair must sign its creation.
Key Takeaway

anchor.workspace gives typed access to methods and account fetchers, reducing boilerplate and errors in client code.

screens.title: Interacting: building and sending instructions
screens.narratorSegment: Anchor's method builder offers a chainable A P I to create and send an instruction. The typical pattern uses program. methods. () which returns a builder configured by the IDL. Then you call accounts({...}) to supply the account public keys required by the instruction's context. If any newly created accounts must sign, include their keypairs in signers([...]). Finally, call rpc() to send the transaction to the cluster. As a concrete example from my-counter-app: program. methods. initialize(). accounts({ counterAccount: counterAccount. publicKey, user: provider. wallet. publicKey, systemProgram: anchor. web3. SystemProgram. programId }). signers([counterAccount]). rpc(); This sequence creates the counter account, signs the creation with the counterAccount keypair, and submits the transaction. A common misconception is that signers are only needed for fee payment; rather, signers are required whenever the instruction requires the private key corresponding to a public key used in the transaction, such as account creation. After rpc() resolves, use program. account. counter. fetch(counterAccount. publicKey) to read the account state and confirm initialization. Closing reflection: what are the consequences of providing the wrong account public key in accounts()? How will the runtime respond?

keyIdea.title: Instruction flow
keyIdea.text: Use program.methods + accounts + signers + rpc to build and send instructions; then fetch account state to verify behavior.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.4 › Sending Instructions
Chainable API

The builder pattern helps you assemble an instruction with accounts, signers, and finally send it with rpc.

Concrete example
// initialize a counter account
await program.methods
  .initialize()
  .accounts({
    counterAccount: counterAccount.publicKey,
    user: provider.wallet.publicKey,
    systemProgram: anchor.web3.SystemProgram.programId,
  })
  .signers([counterAccount])
  .rpc();
Fetch and verify

After sending an instruction, fetch the account to check state changes:

const account = await program.account.counter.fetch(counterAccount.publicKey);
console.log(account.count.toString());
Common mistake
Providing the wrong account public key or forgetting a required account will cause the transaction to fail at runtime with an account validation error.
Key Takeaway

Construct instructions using the IDL-driven builder and always verify state with a fetch after rpc completes.

screens.title: TypeScript test example from my-counter-app
screens.narratorSegment: The provided TypeScript tests illustrate the full cycle of provider setup, program reference, account generation, instruction calls, and validation via fetch and assertions. First the test suite uses anchor. AnchorProvider. env() to get a provider configured for the local cluster, and anchor. setProvider(provider) to apply it. Next, anchor. workspace. MyCounterApp yields a typed Program object generated from the IDL. The tests then generate a new Keypair for the counter account and call initialize with the new account listed in accounts and included in signers so its creation is authorized. After rpc resolves, the test fetches the account with program. account. counter. fetch and asserts the initial count equals zero. Subsequent tests call program. methods. increment() and fetch the account again to assert increments. This pattern demonstrates how you can write repeatable, automated checks that run under anchor test against your local validator. A common misconception is that anchor test only runs unit tests — in Anchor it runs full integration-style tests against the validator. As you follow these tests, notice how the IDL and workspace reduce manual serialization work and make assertions easier. Closing reflection: how would you modify a test to check an error path, like reaching a maximum count?

keyIdea.title: Test pattern
keyIdea.text: TypeScript tests using anchor.AnchorProvider and anchor.workspace run integration tests against the local validator and validate program state changes.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.4 › Test Example
Test structure

Provider, workspace, account generation, rpc calls, fetches, and assertions form a repeatable test pattern.

Key snippet
const provider = anchor.AnchorProvider.env();
anchor.setProvider(provider);
const program = anchor.workspace.MyCounterApp as Program;
const counterAccount = anchor.web3.Keypair.generate();

await program.methods
  .initialize()
  .accounts({
    counterAccount: counterAccount.publicKey,
    user: provider.wallet.publicKey,
    systemProgram: anchor.web3.SystemProgram.programId,
  })
  .signers([counterAccount])
  .rpc();
Assertions and logs
After actions, fetch the account and assert values. The test logs also show program msg! outputs which help trace logic during execution.
Error testing
To test an error path, temporarily adjust program logic to make the error reachable, then run anchor test and assert that the error message is thrown as expected.
Key Takeaway

screens.title: Signers vs PDAs
screens.narratorSegment: Understanding who must sign a transaction is crucial for correct account creation and access control. A keypair has an associated private key and can sign transactions; when you create an account with #[account(init)], the designated keypair must sign, so include it in signers([...]). Program Derived Addresses, or PDAs, on the other hand, are derived deterministically from seeds and a program ID and do not have private keys; they cannot sign. Instead, programs use invoke_signed with the PDA seeds to authorize actions. A common source of confusion is trying to place a PDA in the signers array — that will not work because PDAs cannot sign. Using PDAs is useful for program-owned accounts where the program itself controls authority, while generating and passing a new Keypair is the right approach for client-created accounts that must sign their creation. Example: counterAccount in our tests is a generated Keypair and must appear in signers. If you changed the design to use a PDA for the counter, the client would not include it in signers and the program would use the PDA seeds to create or access it. Closing reflection: when designing ownership and authority, ask whether the on-chain program or an external signer should control the account.

screens.title: Common pitfalls and debugging tips
screens.narratorSegment: When working through the build, deploy, and test loop you will encounter a handful of recurring issues. First, stale builds: if you edit Rust source but skip anchor build, your deploy will push an older. so and tests will appear to fail for no obvious reason. The fix is simple: always run anchor build after code changes. Second, CLI configuration: ensure solana config get lists localhost when using a local validator; otherwise deployments and RPC calls will target the wrong cluster. Third, signer errors: account creation often fails because the required keypair was not included in signers — remember that #[account(init)] requires the new account's keypair to sign creation. Fourth, incorrect account metas: passing the wrong public key in accounts() will produce runtime account mismatch errors. Use program msg! logs liberally in Rust to surface internal state during tests. A practical debugging workflow: confirm the validator is running, re-run anchor build, check anchor deploy output for program ID, run anchor test and scan program logs and fetch results. These checks quickly narrow down most failures. Final reflective question: which of these steps would you automate in a local development script to reduce manual errors?

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you'll learn the practical, repeatable workflow for taking an Anchor Rust program from source code to a running program you can call from a client. We'll cover compiling your Rust into BPF bytecode using the Anchor toolchain, running a local Solana validator so you can test without network fees, and deploying the compiled program with anchor deploy. Then we will walk through writing a minimal TypeScript client that uses the generated IDL to build and send transactions, and finally how to fetch on-chain account state to assert behavior. This matters because development speed and confidence come from a tight loop: change code, build, deploy locally, run tests, and inspect state. A concrete example you'll follow is the my-counter-app — we build it with anchor build, run solana-test-validator, deploy with anchor deploy, then use a TypeScript test to initialize and increment a counter account and assert its value. Common pitfalls include forgetting to build before deploying, not starting the local validator, or not including required signers when creating accounts. By the end you'll understand the commands, the artifacts produced like. so and IDL files, and the client calls you need to send instructions and read program state. Ready to start this practical workflow and see a program run locally?

These objectives map to the hands-on workflow you'll practice. First, you will compile an Anchor program into BPF bytecode so it can run on Solana. That includes running anchor build and inspecting the produced. so and IDL files to confirm the program's interface. Second, you'll set up a local Solana validator using solana-test-validator. This creates an isolated, resettable blockchain environment with a faucet so you can test transactions without real funds. Third, you'll deploy an Anchor program to that local validator using anchor deploy and ensure the program ID is written or updated in Anchor. toml. Fourth, you'll write a basic TypeScript client that uses anchor. workspace and the generated IDL to construct and send instructions. Each objective emphasizes not just the command but why it matters: compilation produces the runnable artifact, the validator protects the public network and accelerates iteration, deploy publishes your code to the cluster you control, and the client connects on-chain logic with UI or tests. As you study, think about what could go wrong at each step and how logs, CLI output, and the IDL help you diagnose problems.

This second objectives panel emphasizes the practical skills for testing and diagnosing issues. You'll run anchor test to execute TypeScript tests against your local validator, observe msg! logs emitted by the program, and confirm assertions using fetched account state. You'll also practice error testing: how to create a scenario that triggers a program-defined error, such as a counter overflow, so you can verify custom error handling in your program. Finally, you'll practice the iterative loop of editing Rust code, running anchor build, deploying to the local validator, and re-running tests to confirm fixes. Knowing how to reproduce an error locally and how to read the CLI output reduces debugging time. A common misconception is treating anchor deploy as a substitute for anchor build; remember that deploy sends whatever is already built, so always build after source changes. These objectives prepare you to run reliable local experiments and to write client code that intentionally validates program behavior.

Compilation transforms your human-written Rust code with Anchor macros into the binary format Solana nodes execute. When you run anchor build, Anchor orchestrates a Rust cargo build that targets BPF, producing a shared object file — the. so — and a generated IDL JSON that describes your program's public interface. The. so is the deployable executable that the cluster stores and runs. The IDL is a machine-readable contract: it lists instructions, each instruction's accounts and types, and any custom errors. A practical example is the my-counter-app: after a successful build you will find a my_counter_app. so file in target/deploy and an IDL at target/idl/my_counter_app. json. Inspecting the IDL helps client code know how to marshal arguments and which account addresses to include. A common misconception is that only the. so matters. In practice, the IDL is equally important for client development because it enables typed clients via anchor. workspace and prevents malformed transactions. As a quick check, build your program and verify both artifacts exist. If compilation fails, read Rust compiler messages and Anchor attribute hints; they usually tell you which module or attribute caused the error. The key takeaway is: build produces both runtime code and the contract description you need for client-side interaction.

A local validator gives you a private Solana cluster on your machine for development and testing. To start, open a terminal and run solana-test-validator. This spins up a node with a faucet so you can request test SOL and it runs in a temporary ledger that resets when you stop it. While it's running, configure your Solana CLI to use the local endpoint with solana config set --url localhost, and confirm using solana config get. The benefit is immediate feedback: transactions you send from a client or anchor test execute quickly and you can inspect msg! logs. A common practical concern is ledger persistence: by default the test validator is ephemeral; if you need a persistent ledger you can pass flags to save the ledger to disk. Another misconception is believing the validator replicates network conditions exactly — it does not emulate mainnet traffic, but it provides a safe, isolated environment for functionally testing program logic. Example use: start the validator, deploy your compiled. so with anchor deploy, then run anchor test or your TypeScript client to verify initialization and increments. Closing question: when you see an RPC connection error, what three CLI checks will you perform first to ensure the validator is reachable?

Deployment publishes your compiled. so to a configured Solana cluster. Using Anchor's CLI, anchor deploy reads your Anchor. toml to determine program IDs and the keypairs used for deployment. When you run anchor deploy against a local validator, Anchor will upload the. so and sign the deployment transaction with the provided keypair. For a fresh deployment Anchor may generate and then update Anchor. toml with the program ID. A practical example is deploying the my-counter-app: ensure you have run anchor build, that solana-test-validator is running, and that the Solana CLI points to localhost. Then run anchor deploy from the project root. Watch the CLI output for the Program ID and any error messages. A frequent mistake is deploying an out-of-date. so because the developer skipped anchor build after changes. Another point: Anchor handles signing and keypairs for you, but be aware of which keypair is used for deployment and where it is stored. After a successful deploy, your program is live on your local validator and ready to receive instructions from a client or tests. Ask yourself: did the deploy output a program ID and did Anchor. toml reflect it?

The Anchor client stack provides utilities that make calling your deployed program straightforward. In TypeScript, anchor. AnchorProvider. env() constructs a provider that ties together a connection, a wallet, and default options. When you call anchor. setProvider(provider), Anchor's client functions will use that environment for RPCs. Most importantly, anchor. workspace. MyCounterApp is a typed object generated from the IDL that exposes program methods and account accessors. This typed workspace saves you from manually constructing instruction data and account metas. For example, after setting the provider, you can get the program reference: const program = anchor. workspace. MyCounterApp as Program. From there, program. methods. initialize() builds the initialize instruction according to the IDL. A common misconception is that you can call methods without the IDL; while possible manually, the IDL ensures argument order and account names match the program. A concrete scenario: generate a counterAccount keypair, call initialize with signers([counterAccount]), then fetch the account with program. account. counter. fetch(counterAccount. publicKey) to read the count. When tests run with anchor test, Anchor sets environment variables so provider. env picks up the localhost cluster automatically. Reflect: how does the IDL reduce mistakes when building transactions?

Anchor's method builder offers a chainable A P I to create and send an instruction. The typical pattern uses program. methods. () which returns a builder configured by the IDL. Then you call accounts({...}) to supply the account public keys required by the instruction's context. If any newly created accounts must sign, include their keypairs in signers([...]). Here are the essential concepts to retain from this chapter. First, compilation turns Anchor Rust into BPF bytecode and produces both a. so file and an IDL JSON. The. so is the executable artifact, and the IDL describes the program interface for clients. Second, solana-test-validator provides a local, isolated cluster with a faucet that enables fast iteration without real funds; configure your Solana CLI to point to localhost to use it. Third, deployment with anchor deploy publishes the compiled. so to the configured cluster and updates Anchor. toml with the program ID for client targeting. Keeping these three ideas front of mind will help you move quickly from code to running program to client interactions.
